Capitellidae are commonly found, and it is a bit surprising there
is no common name for the group. They are easily recognized,
for the most part, by the division of the body into an anterior
region with capillary chaetae only and a posterior region with
Jong-handled hooks. However, the taxonomy within the group
and assessing relationships among taxa presents significant diffi-
culties. This may in part be due to their relative simplicity when
it comes to external anatomy. The body is a simple cylindrical
shape resembling that of many Clitellata. They range in size from
less than 10 mm to more than 200 mm and, in life, the body is
usually bright red (Pl. 10d).

The head of Capitellidae has no appendages and is formed from
the prostomium and peristomium (Eisig, 1887). The prostomi-
um is highly variable in shape, but is often a short, blunt cone
(Pl. 10d, Figs. 48.1a-c, 48.2a-c). On the prostomium, there may
be one or more pairs of simple eyespots (Fig. 48.1c) and there is
usually a pair of eversible nuchal organs (Eisig, 1887). Develop-
mental studies (Bookhout, 1957) indicate that the peristomium
forms a complete ring (Figs. 48.1a, c), contra Rouse and Fauchald
(1997) who stated it is limited to the buccal region. The ring-
like nature is very clear in most Capitellidae, but many older
works state that the peristomium has chaetae. Warren (1991) has
shown there is a ring-like peristomium in Capitella that is often
obscured by contraction of the body during fixation. This needs
to be considered when consulting most literature on the group.
For example, Baldia is unusual in that the mouth supposedly
has the peristomium in front of it and the first segment imme-
diately behind (Garwood and Bamber, 1988); however, these
authors also argue the same condition exists in Capitella. Pos-
sibly their specimens of Baldia may have suffered from the same
contraction artefacts that appear to affect Capitella.
Capitellidae have historically often been regarded as having
an achaetous first segment (Fauchald, 1977), but in most cas-
es this ‘segment’ is the peristomium. Given that the body is
divided into a thorax (Figs. 48.1a, 48.2c) and abdomen, and that
the former is of taxonomic value, many counts of the number
of thoracic segment number may be in error. The presence of
an achaetous first segment is accepted for Leocapitellides, some

Mastobranchus, Pseudonotomastus, and Scyphoproctus (Magalhaes
and Blake, 2020; Silva and Zacagnini Amaral, 2019). The num-
ber of thoracic segments is often not easily determined because
there may be transitional segments, or no change in the chaetal
forms between the two body regions. This suggests that the divi-
sion between thorax and abdomen is associated with internal
features and may not correlate well with external anatomy. In
some taxa, the epidermis may be thick and rugose over'the tho-
racic region and changes to a much thinner epidermis in the
abdomen. In some cases, use of stains like methyl green will
show marked differences in glandular patterns that separate the
thoracic and abdominal regions much more clearly than chaetal
distributions (Ewing, 1984b).
Difficulties in properly identifying the thoracic region
notwithstanding, the thorax area usually has around 8-19
chaetigerous segments (Figs. 48.1a, b, 48.2a-c). The parapo-
dia are essentially absent in that there are simple grooves from
which the chaetae emerge. In general, these thoracic chaetae
are simple or winged capillaries in both noto- and neuropodia
(e.g, Dasybranchus), or there may be a uniramous first chaetiger
(Fig, 48.1a). Also, in many taxa, there may be posterior thoracic
chaetigers with long-handled hooded hooks in both noto- and
neuropodia (e.g. Mediomastus), or there may be a mixture of
hooded hooks and capillary chaetae (e.g. Capitella). In some taxa
(e.g, Capitella), there are distinct genital spines in chaetigers 8
and 9 (Fig. 48.2a). Amastigos and Baldia are unique among Capitel-
lidae in lacking capillary chaetae in the thorax and instead have
hooks all along this region and the remaining body, though tho-
racic and abdominal regions are still discernible (Garwood and
Bamber, 1988; Piltz, 1976).
‘The abdominal region has many more segments than the tho-
rax and abdominal segments are usually longer. The parapodial
rami are elongate tori (Pl. 10d, Figs. 48.1a, 48.2c), with those of
the neuropodia usually longer than the notopodia. In general,
both rami of all abdominal chaetigers bear long-handled hood-
ed hooks (Fig. 48.14), though in some cases there may be some
capillary chaetae in the notopodia (e.g. Mastobranchus). In addi-
tion, several pre-anal segments of taxa such as Scyphoproctus may
have stout spines in the notopodia. The long-handled hooks have
a capitium (rows of fine teeth) over a rostrum (= main fang) and
a distinctive hood with an opening for the rostrum (Fig. 48.14)
